03 — GLP1R agonist · the complete history

This document tells the whole story of the GLP1R agonist campaign, from the scraped challenge page to the submitted twenty designs. It names every tool, every decision, and the reason for each. The companion records are lineage.json (the campaign history the website renders), notes/ (the research and the per-round records), campaigns/ (the working dirs and every script), records/ (the score and prescreen tables) and submission/ (the shipped file and the two method texts).

Status: the repo marks the challenge complete — twelve campaigns, 800 scored designs, a twenty-design file built on 2026-10-23, two days before the 2026-10-25 deadline (../../README.md, the previous README). Nothing here is wet-lab validated. No upload receipt and no assay result is recorded anywhere in the tree; everything below is computational evidence.

1. The target and what "agonist" means

The brief was captured on 2026-10-18 from the competition hub and the challenge page (notes/brief.md). The target:

field value
target human GLP1R, UniProt P43220-1
segment residues 24–432 (409 aa): the extracellular domain, seven transmembrane helices, the start of the tail
supply receptor in DDM/CHS detergent (assay 13944-H18H-DD, N-FLAG / C-His; proprietary thermostabilising mutations not listed — the public sequence is wild type)
recommended epitope the peptide-binding groove of the extracellular domain — where GLP-1, exendin-4 and semaglutide dock
structure reference PDB 6X18, chain R
conditions none — no species, no pH

Two objectives, in the organizers' order:

  1. Affinity against human GLP1R, measured on the detergent receptor.
  2. Activation — a confirmed agonist in a cell-based reporter assay (cAMP → secreted alkaline phosphatase → luminescence, compared with untreated cells and a reference agonist).

The objective is functional, and that is the whole difficulty. A binder that does not activate does not count. This is the one thing that separates challenge 3 from every other binder challenge in this repo: the second objective is not a property of the interface strength, it is a property of the pose. The receptor is a switch, and the question is not "does the design hold the switch" but "does it push it".

Our reading of the brief, recorded before any generation (notes/strategies.md, submission/methodology.md). The organizers recommend the groove. Our reading of the published mechanism was that the groove is only the address half of the job, and that the message half — the part that actually flips the switch — sits deeper, where the hormone's own N-terminus reaches into the transmembrane bundle. So the campaign targeted the junction between the two: the place where the extracellular domain hands over to the membrane-embedded part. That split reading, address versus message, is the single decision the rest of the project executes.

2. The biology in plain words: a switch, and why the groove alone is a trap

What GLP1R is. A receptor sitting in the membrane of a cell, of the family called class-B G-protein-coupled receptors. "Coupled to a G protein" means: when the right molecule binds the outside of the receptor, the part of the receptor inside the cell changes shape and grabs a messenger protein (Gs), which starts a chemical cascade (cAMP). GLP1R is the incretin receptor — the one the GLP-1 drug class (semaglutide and relatives) targets to control blood sugar and appetite.

What the natural agonist does. The hormone GLP-1 is a 30-residue peptide, and it binds in two places at once (notes/research-brief.md, citing 10.1016/j.cell.2016.05.023 and 10.1074/jbc.M109.033829):

  • its C-terminal helix sits in the groove of the extracellular domain — a cradle that sticks up above the membrane. This is the address: it is what makes the hormone stick to this receptor and not another.
  • its N-terminus threads down into the transmembrane bundle, past the extracellular loops, into a pocket inside the receptor. This is the message: these are the contacts that move the helices.

On activation the whole receptor rearranges. In the resting (apo) state the extracellular domain lies down on the transmembrane part, burying 928 Å² of surface; in the peptide-bound active state it stands up along the peptide, that interface shrinks to roughly 350 Å², the domain's tip travels 18–28 Å, and the sixth transmembrane helix develops the kink that lets Gs dock (10.1038/s41467-020-14934-5; 10.1038/nature22394).

Why the groove alone is a trap — the single most important fact in this challenge. Occupying the groove is enough to block the hormone and not enough to replace it. The record is unambiguous (notes/research-brief.md):

  • the only published de-novo GLP1R extracellular-domain miniproteins (dGl1_024, IC50 61 nM; mGl1_008, IC50 39 nM; made with RFdiffusion plus MetaGen and screened by yeast display over roughly 17,000 designs) are antagonists (10.1101/2025.03.23.644666);
  • the same study's companion receptors — GLP1R, GIPR, GCGR, CGRPR — all yielded antagonists; an agonist was obtained only for a different receptor, MRGPRX1;
  • of 13 published anti-GLP1R antibodies, the one agonist among them was an antibody fused to a GLP-1 peptide; the antibody part alone did not activate (10.1080/19420862.2021.1893425).

Non-peptide agonists exist and they all touch the membrane-embedded part, never the groove alone: orforglipron binds the upper bundle against the domain's Trp33 lid plus ECL2 and TM1/2/3/7 (a partial, Gs-biased agonist), danuglipron overlaps the GLP-1 site and reproduces GLP-1 pharmacology, and TT-OAD2 sits at the ECL3/TM6–7 rim (partial and slow) (10.1073/pnas.2014879117; 10.1016/j.molcel.2020.09.020; 10.1038/s41586-019-1902-z).

Two public challenge-3 repositories were found during the research pass, both targeting the extracellular groove, and both state outright that they do not engineer activation and do not expect their binders to activate. One of them also recorded the trap that follows from using a cut-down target: binders designed against the extracellular domain alone clash into the transmembrane bundle that was omitted from the design target (notes/research-brief.md). That became a rule here: generate against a fragment if you must, but always fold against the full receptor.

A designed agonist versus the natural hormone. Both are peptides or small proteins, and they differ in what matters:

GLP-1, the hormone our designed molecules
origin evolved; a human hormone designed in days by five generators
size 30 residues 13–96 residues in the submitted set
what it touches all four sub-sites: groove 6/6, junction 4/4, TM pocket 4/4, ECL3 5/8 — 19 receptor residues in all the best in our pool reproduce 6 of those 19
evidence of agonism decades of pharmacology a geometry score calibrated on four experimental structures
what decides the clinic the organizers' cAMP reporter assay

What the competition actually measures, and what it does not. Binding is measured first; only confirmed binders go into the activation assay. So a design must survive two gates in the real world, and the second one has no public in-silico predictor at all. That absence is the subject of chapter 4.

3. The reference structures and what we measured on them

Why structures matter here. A single receptor molecule is far too small to photograph. Structures come from X-ray crystallography or cryo-electron microscopy: many copies of the molecule, a beam, a diffraction or image series, and mathematics that turns the pattern into atom positions. Every geometric number in this project is measured on such files with our own scripts; nothing is estimated.

The primary file: 6X18 (2.1 Å, 10.1016/j.molcel.2020.09.020) — GLP-1 bound to GLP1R with the Gs protein attached: the active state, caught with the hormone in place. Our own read of the file (notes/groove-contacts.md, produced by campaigns/c1-two-domain/scripts/analyze_6x18.py):

  • chains A (355 residues), B (338), G (56), N (126), P (30), R (384);
  • chain R is the receptor, aligned identity 0.969 against the challenge segment in UniProt numbering — close enough to use directly;
  • chain P is GLP-1, 30 residues;
  • 56 receptor residues sit within 4.5 Å of the peptide, and they fall into three zones: the extracellular groove (residues 30–145), the ECD/TMD junction (148–241) and the transmembrane pocket (297–392). The full list is in that note; the hotspot file is inputs/groove-hotspots.csv.

Those 56 residues were cut into the four sub-site sets that every screen in this project uses (campaigns/c1-two-domain/scripts/screen_folds_c3.py):

sub-site residues (UniProt P43220 numbering) what it is
groove D67, Y69, Y88, W91, R121, E128 the address: the cradle on top
junction K197, Q210, Q221, Q234 where the domain hands over to the membrane part
TM pocket T298, N300, I309, I313 the top of the bundle, on the hormone's path inward
ECL3 / TM6–7 376, 377, 380, 381, 384, E387, 388, 391 the loop region that reorganizes on activation; 387 is a published reach anchor

The calibration ladder. Four more experimental structures were used, not as design targets but as a measuring stick for the activation scorer (chapter 4): 6X18 (GLP-1, full agonist), 6B3J (exendin-P5, the known G-protein-biased full agonist), 7LLL (exendin-4, full agonist) and 9IVG (GLP-1(9-36), the weak partial agonist metabolite). Their numbers are in notes/agonism-geometry-2026-10-20.md.

Supporting files named in the research brief (notes/research-brief.md): 3IOL for the extracellular-domain groove contacts (the hormone's hydrophobic face Leu25/Phe28/Ile29/Leu32/Val33 packing the groove, Val33 hydrogen-bonding Arg121, Lys26 to Glu128), 5NX2 (active-like), 6LN2 (peptide-free, closed extracellular domain — the resting state), 6XOX / 6X1A / 6X19 (small-molecule complexes) and 6ORV (TT-OAD2).

One measurement that saved the project from a silent error. A contact depth means nothing if the folded receptor is in the wrong state: a closed, self-inhibited receptor makes unrelated contacts look like reach. So the folds were checked against 6X18 directly — for the campaign-1 leader e1-r0025 the intra-receptor CA distances agree with 6X18 within 2–4 Å at residues 67/91/121–300/234, i.e. Boltz folded the receptor active with the depth-capped MSA (notes/strategies.md, campaigns/c1-two-domain/LEARNINGS.md). The learnings file states the rule plainly: verify the receptor state before trusting any depth metric, every time.

4. The doctrine: no tool predicts agonism, so build and calibrate one

The problem, stated. The published record says confidence scores do not separate agonists from antagonists (A. Muratspahic et al., Nature 2026, as quoted in notes/agonism-geometry-2026-10-20.md). An independent October 2026 benchmark found that interface-confidence scores have zero association with epitope engagement at all (notes/scoring-upgrades-2026-10-19.md). And the project's own research pass found no open-weight GLP-1R potency model and no trustworthy open PPI-affinity head. In short: the metric that would answer objective 2 did not exist, and the metrics that did exist could not even be trusted to say where a design binds.

Three consequences were adopted as doctrine, each of them recorded with its evidence:

  1. The designed-site contact screen is mandatory, for every design, from every generator. Confidence numbers rank, contacts decide.
  2. A generator's own metrics are never a filter. Two measurements forced this. BoltzGen's internal ipTM called its best junction designs weak at 0.21–0.41 while our independent screen put the same designs at ipSAE 0.77–0.86 (campaigns/c3-boltzgen-cyclic/README.md). And BindCraft2 accepted 0 of 50 trajectories by its own gate — yet among its rejected raw output was the best design in the challenge at that date (c5-bc2-l18_bfe509d11b1b8f27, ipSAE 0.861, a two-domain HIT; notes/best-per-campaign.md). A generator's gate would have thrown away the winner.
  3. Rank on metrics that were measured against outcomes. The screen was upgraded on 2026-10-19 from the 3,766-binder meta-analysis (Overath et al. 2025, bioRxiv 10.1101/2025.08.14.670059), which found ipSAE_min the single best predictor of real binding; the screen now extracts ipSAE, ipSAE_d0chn, ipTM_af, pDockQ, pDockQ2 and LIS from every IPSAE report, plus binder pLDDT and inter-chain PAE (notes/scoring-upgrades-2026-10-19.md). The same pass fixed a column mislabel: what the screen called pDockQ2 had been reading pDockQ.

4.1 The activation-geometry gate

On 2026-10-20 a community scan found the first usable activation scorer: an unmerged but openly readable file, scripts/activation_geometry.py in pull request #98 of charleneleong-ai/ai4science. It does not predict agonism statistically — it measures the activating geometry directly, feature by feature, with cutoffs declared before any design exists. It was run verbatim, never modified. (The third-party copy was removed from the repo in commit 33f8592; it runs from ~/c3-work/c8-agonism/scorers/activation_geometry.py, which is outside the repository. The scorer's own comments are the source for the parameters below.)

The six features — the GLP-1 message region's pharmacophore, ranked by the mutational cost of losing each one, all in UniProt P43220 numbering, with cutoffs set 1.0 Å looser than the distance the native complex achieves:

# feature what the design must place, and where cutoff
1 anion_to_R190 a carboxylate oxygen at Arg190's guanidinium nitrogens 4.2 Å
2 aromatic_at_Y148 an aromatic ring at Tyr148 (also 141/144/388) 4.5 Å
3 small_at_W306 any atom at Trp306's ring edge 4.5 Å
4 hbond_to_Q234 a hydrogen-bond partner at Gln234's amide 4.0 Å
5 hydrophobe_at_E387 a hydrophobic contact at Glu387/388 4.5 Å
6 ecl3_contact any contact at 372/373/380 4.5 Å

Plus a depth. How far below the mouth of the receptor the ligand reaches. The mouth is defined by the receptor itself — the centroid of the vestibule-rim residues 205, 210, 211, 214, 215, 221, 298, 299, 300, 372, 380 — and the direction is the vector from that centroid to the centroid of the pocket floor (234, 237, 241, 306, 310, 313, 387). The deepest ligand atom projected on that axis is the reported depth. No membrane is modelled, which is why the axis is taken from the protein.

The tiers, straight from the scorer's constants: wrong_face if more contacts are intracellular than either extracellular-domain or transmembrane; deep if the depth is ≥ 16.0 Å and at least 3 features are satisfied; shelf if depth ≥ 10.0 Å; otherwise groove.

Calibration: reproduced, not trusted. The gate was run on four experimental structures before it was allowed to score a single design, and it reproduced the source's numbers exactly, including the known quirks (notes/agonism-geometry-2026-10-20.md):

structure ligand features depth the quirk
6X18 GLP-1, full agonist 6/6 20.59 Å —
6B3J exendin-P5, full agonist 4/6 23.57 Å misses the R190 anion at 5.03 Å — it is the known G-protein-biased agonist
7LLL exendin-4, full agonist 4/6 18.92 Å misses the Q234 bond at 4.93 Å
9IVG GLP-1(9-36), weak partial 1/6 14.15 Å —
— GLP-1 16-36 (groove-only control) 0/6 7.3 Å the source's own negative control

That ladder is what gives the gate meaning: a design's score means the same thing the lab's agonists and partial agonists mean. A full agonist reads 4–6 features at 18.9–23.6 Å; a groove-only ligand reads 0 features at 7 Å.

The gate's declared limit, and the mitigation. The scorer scores the pose it is given, not whether the design would adopt it. The mitigation is pose agreement: every design is folded five times and the gate is run on every sample, so the gate reports two separate figures — the feature count from the best sample, and how many of the five samples land in the deep tier. The notation 6/6 d19.2 5/5 therefore reads: the best sample reproduced all six contacts at 19.2 Å, and all five samples were deep.

4.2 The second, harsher lens, and what it caught

A design can pile up contacts without inserting anything. To catch that, a second scorer measures how much of the hormone's whole footprint each design reproduces (campaigns/c3-boltzgen-cyclic/scripts/agonist_likeness.py, documented in notes/agonist-likeness-2026-10-20.md). GLP-1 in 6X18 touches 19 receptor residues: groove 6/6, junction 4/4, TM pocket 4/4, ECL3 5/8. The metric is the fraction of those 19 a design reproduces, and it is harsh on purpose.

The result, over 644 folded designs (notes/likeness-finding-2026-10-22.md):

  • no design in the pool is agonist-like in absolute terms. The pool ceiling is 6 of 19; the top-ranked full-geometry designs reproduce 3 to 5 of 19.
  • Four designs hit the 6/19 ceiling — and the depth check disqualified three of them immediately. Their apparent reach came from wrapping poses, insertion depths of 57 to 74 Å: a binder lying across the receptor, not inserting into it. Their pattern was an artifact of counting contacts on a molecule draped over the target.
  • Exactly one design survived both lenses at the time: c12-mpnn-b13-d01-v3 (6/6 at 23.9 Å, 5/5 agreement, likeness at the ceiling, ipSAE 0.855). It was swapped into the twenty on 2026-10-22 and then swapped back out by the 2026-10-23 pure-score rebuild (chapter 8).
  • An earlier run of the same metric over 146 designs had put the ranking's leaders at 0.26–0.32 and noted that the likeness ranking disagrees with the affinity ranking (notes/agonist-likeness-2026-10-20.md). It does; the disagreement is the wrap-pose problem.

The wrap-pose threshold was fixed at 30 Å and applied as a penalty, not a veto: in the final rubric a 6/6 design deeper than 30 Å loses a full point of activation credit.

The methodological conclusion, recorded verbatim in the finding note: a screen can only discard, it cannot supply a feature the generator never produced. The likeness dead-end said the pool already contained everything groove/junction conditioning could reach, and that the remaining upside lay in aiming generation at the pattern — which is the shelved reward-guidance work of chapter 6.

4.3 The instrument matrix

instrument what it was asked what it read action taken

5. The pipeline, stage by stage

Each stage states its hypothesis, the numbers it produced, and the decision that followed.

The whole pipeline as a funnel: 800 designs from five generators plus one re-sequencer, the filter at every stage, and the tool behind every metric. Green chips are free CPU steps that run in seconds, orange chips cost GPU minutes, and the pink chip is the expensive verification round — the five-sample Boltz-2 co-fold of every design against the full 409-residue receptor, which every number downstream is computed from. The note at the bottom marks the loop that fed champions back in: interface-pinned SolubleMPNN re-sequencing, which ran three times and produced 154 of the 800 designs.

Stage 1 — Generation. Hypothesis: the activating pose needs the junction, so conditioning generation on the junction will produce it more often than conditioning on the groove. Procedure: five independent generators, each a different bet on the same question, generating against a fragment of the receptor (RFdiffusion3 needs the target under ~250 residues to run at all) or against the annotated full construct. Numbers: 800 designs scored in total, by generator family:

colour in the funnel generator designs what the conditioning asked for
blue RFD4-Proteina (hosted) 401 three rounds: the deep message region (256), the ECD–TMD junction block (73), the deep region at 40–70 aa (72)
green SolubleMPNN re-sequencing 154 not a generator: re-sequences existing champion backbones with the interface pinned (40 + 33 + 81)
lime BoltzGen 145 cyclic peptides at the junction (55), 20–24 aa peptides (30), the junction recipe at scale (60)
amber RFdiffusion3 67 miniproteins, contig 60-100, against the groove+junction set and then the junction alone (inputs/rfd3-e1.json, inputs/rfd3-e1b.json)
cyan BindCraft2 18 15–18 aa peptides at the junction, gates relaxed so raw output reaches our screen
pink EvoBind 15 peptides designed from sequence alone, no backbone, no template

The counts come from records/selection-scores-2026-10-23.csv, whose eleven family labels sum to 800 (337 + 73 + 72 + 67 + 60 + 55 + 40 + 33 + 30 + 18 + 15). The table above regroups them by what made the sequence: the selector's 337 "rfd4-proteina" rows are the 256 deep-round designs plus their 81 re-sequenced variants, because both share the c12 prefix, so those 81 are counted under SolubleMPNN here (40 + 33 + 81 = 154) and the RFD4 slice holds only the three generation rounds (256 + 73 + 72 = 401).

Decision: the junction conditioning won on both generators that tested it, and the hosted RFD4-Proteina rounds won on every axis. Both findings are in chapter 6.

Stage 2 — The co-fold (the expensive step). Hypothesis: a Boltz-2 co-fold against the full 409-residue construct, never a fragment, is the only honest way to see whether a design clashes into the part of the receptor the generator never saw. Procedure (submission/design-method.md): Boltz-2 2.2.1, 5 diffusion samples per design, seed 42, binder as chain A, the full construct as chain B, receptor MSA depth-capped at 1024 rows. Numbers: the uncapped server MSA needed 14.65 GiB and was killed by the memory watchdog; fetched once and capped, folds run at about 90 s and ~11.7 GiB (campaigns/c1-two-domain/LEARNINGS.md, campaigns/c1-two-domain/scripts/fetch_msas.py). Decision: this became the one shared pipeline — every design from every generator is re-folded here, so all 800 are scored by the same script with the same settings.

Stage 3 — The two-domain binding screen. Hypothesis: a high ipSAE with the binder sitting only on the groove is the known antagonist outcome, so the screen must test the footprint, not just the score. Procedure (campaigns/c1-two-domain/scripts/screen_folds_c3.py): per sample, ipSAE ≥ 0.8 (the line calibrated in challenge 2: below it, nothing bound in the wet lab) and ≥ 1 groove residue within 4.5 Å and ≥ 1 TM-pocket residue within 4.5 Å and zero atom pairs closer than 2.0 Å. A design meeting the contact test but not the score is labelled groove-only. Numbers: the campaign table totals 222 two-domain HITs across the twelve campaigns (notes/campaign-tables-2026-10-23.md; its per-campaign figures do not always match the campaign notes — see chapter 11). Decision: kept as the binding objective's record for every campaign; the clash column is what catches the trap the public repos fell into.

Stage 4 — The activation-geometry gate. Hypothesis: a design that independently reproduces the hormone's message-region geometry is the best available bet on agonism. Procedure: the calibrated gate of chapter 4, run on every one of the five samples of every design (campaigns/c8-deep-junction/scripts/rescore-all.py, which parses the scorer's report lines with regexes so column padding cannot shift fields, and caches per-sample rows because the per-sample scoring is the expensive half — one scorer subprocess per model). Numbers: 87 of 800 designs carry the full 6/6 pattern on at least one sample; the first full rescore (2026-10-20) covered 213 designs and 1,065 samples and found six. Decision: the gate became the primary ranking axis, and its verdict redirected generation twice — campaign 8 exists only because the gate said the c3 junction recipe produced 4 of the first 6 perfect geometries.

Stage 5 — The wrap-pose check. Hypothesis: deep contact counts can be faked by a binder lying across the receptor. Numbers: 40 of the deep-tier designs in the first rescore sat at depths of 40–68 Å; of the four designs that reached the likeness ceiling, three were wrapping at 57–74 Å. Decision: a declared 30 Å threshold; beyond it the activation score loses a point, and the flagged designs are not trusted.

Stage 6 — Quality floors, then the composite, then de-duplication. Hypothesis: the composite under-weights the things that stop a design from ever being tested, so those must be hard floors applied before ranking. Procedure (campaigns/c8-deep-junction/scripts/select-top20.py): no design below 63 pLDDT, none below 0.18 pDockQ2, and no low-complexity sequence (residue entropy < 2.5 bits, or a single residue above 45 % of the chain, or a homopolymer run of 6 or more). Then rank by total = 2·A + 1.5·B + 1·E + 0.5·R (chapter 8), then reject any sequence ≥ 90 % identical to one already kept. Numbers: the floors remove 486 of the 800 scored designs and leave 314 eligible. The floors exist because the selector once returned a 24-residue poly-alanine tract that scored 88.4 — the comment in the script says so. Decision: floors first, score second, diversity only as a tie-break.

Stage 7 — The organizers' prescreen. Procedure: the organizers' own public tool, adaptyvbio/binder-prescreen, whose GLP1R reference set is 225 curated entries (215 GLP-1 analogue peptides, 7 antibody chains, 3 peptide-Fc fusions). Numbers: on the shipped twenty (records/prescreen-report-rubric-2026-10-23.csv): 18 pass, 2 return no_reference_signal — both of them peptides (13 and 15 residues), which is the tool's documented blind spot for sequences under 25 residues, not a failure. Target similarity is 0.00 for nineteen of the twenty and 0.095 for the twentieth; every cluster size is 1, so no two entries are duplicates by the platform's own check. An earlier run on 2026-10-21 over 17 lead candidates returned zero flags (9 pass, 8 no_reference_signal). Decision: the file ships.

6. The campaigns (twelve in all)

Each campaign below names its date, strategy, tools and result. The primary record is lineage.json, whose twelve experiments carry the per-step text, the tool list and the outcome for each; the per-campaign working notes are in campaigns/*/README.md and notes/.

The same epitope reached three ways. Left: c13-junction-b43-d02, the 96-residue junction-conditioned RFD4 champion that leads the submission (6/6 at 19.2 Å, all five samples deep, ipSAE 0.918). Middle: c2-run1-b206, the 15-residue EvoBind peptide that reproduces the full pattern at 20.6 Å — the hormone's own depth in 6X18 is 20.59 Å. Right: e1-r0025, the 66-residue RFdiffusion3 miniprotein with the pool's highest ipSAE at 0.933 and 5 of 6 contacts. The receptor is the same full 409-residue construct in all three panels; the designs differ by a factor of six in size and land in the same place. Each panel comes from its own campaign's viewer page, so the receptors were superposed onto the left panel's frame (CA RMSD 5-7 A, the folds' own conformational spread) and all panels share one camera; the binder is magenta, the receptor blue.

Why the numbering has gaps. The campaigns are numbered c1, c2, c3, c5, c6, c7, c8, c9, c12 (twice), c13, c14 — and the gaps have three different explanations:

  • c4 was merged into c3. It ran as c4-junction-scale, 30 more junction designs on the identical spec, and both the lineage record (the chapter whose id is literally c4 inside the c3 experiment) and the README treat it as c3's fourth batch (campaigns/c3-boltzgen-cyclic/README.md).
  • c12 is two entries because the generation round and the re-sequencing pass over its own champions are separate experiments in lineage.json (c12-rfd4-proteina and c12-mpnn-variants), and the selector maps both to the c12 family prefix.
  • c10 and c11 have no record at all. Searching the whole challenge tree and the git history for them returns exactly two artifacts: a prepared generation spec, inputs/rfd3-c11.json ("c11-deep": a local RFdiffusion3 run against the full construct with deep hotspots R118/R178/R275/R276/R277/R283/R357/R361), for which no design, fold or score exists anywhere; and the shelved reward-guided RFD4 plan (notes/rfd4-guidance-plan.md, added 2026-10-22 in commit fa7cb4a, closed the same day in commit 13be510, removed from the tree in commit 33f8592). The record does not say which of those was c10 and which c11, or whether the numbers were simply skipped. What the shelved plan does record is a complete negative: the metric-guidance route — differentiating a soft version of the activation gate against the model's predicted clean state, the only method that would have aimed generation at the pattern instead of filtering into it — was coded, registered and never run, because five attempts were memory-killed (13.29 and 13.30 GiB against a 15.6 GB WSL cap on both the full and the trimmed target, then 19.84, 19.12 and 20.03 GiB after wsl --shutdown raised the VM to 23 GB). The decomposition is recorded too: an eager baseline of ~14.5 GiB plus about 5 GiB that torch.compile adds and compile_lengths=null does not remove. The metric and the config are ready for any machine with 20+ GiB of headroom.

Not every campaign is the same kind of experiment. Three kinds appear below. (1) A new generator at the same site: c1 (RFdiffusion3), c2 (EvoBind), c3 (BoltzGen), c5 (BindCraft2), c12 (RFD4-Proteina). (2) A new region or a new length band with a generator that already works: c7 (20–24 aa), c8 (the c3 recipe at scale), c13 (the junction block on RFD4), c14 (40–70 aa on RFD4). (3) No new generation at all: c6, c9 and c12's variant pass re-sequence backbones that already exist.

C1 — two-domain miniproteins (2026-10-18 → 10-19; partial). Tools: RFdiffusion3, ProteinMPNN, Boltz-2, IPSAE. Strategy S1 of notes/strategies.md: generate miniproteins that dock the groove and extend toward the transmembrane pocket. Three generation experiments — E1 (43 backbones, groove+junction hotspots), E1b (60, junction only), E1b2 (80, the junction repeat) — plus E3, a fixed-interface ProteinMPNN refinement round. 183 backbones generated; 77 designs folded (8 folds lost to memory kills were recovered in a retry pass); 335 samples screened. Result: 39 of 335 samples are two-domain hits across 21 distinct designs. The campaign's decisive measurement is the hotspot comparison: junction-only conditioning gave 25 % two-domain designs in E1b2 against 14 % for groove+junction in E1 — the "split rule" that every later campaign inherited. Best design e1-r0025: ipSAE 0.933, pDockQ2 0.493, a 66-residue binder whose 4.5 Å contact map covers 17 groove residues, 17 junction residues, 5 TM-top residues and 7 ECL3/TM6–7 residues including E387. Two negatives were recorded as carefully as the positive: plain ProteinMPNN re-sequencing collapses to poly-alanine on RFdiffusion3's alanine-rich helices (e1-r0007's chain A is ~45 % alanine), and low_memory_mode=True is a trap on large targets. (Count note: the lineage viewer carries 57 c1 designs, the 10-20 campaign table says 57, the final rescore table says 67, and notes/strategies.md says 77 folded — see chapter 11.)

C2 — peptide agonists with EvoBind (2026-10-19; promising). Tools: EvoBind, Boltz-2, IPSAE. The rationale is the only experimental agonism prior available: EvoBind is the one published pipeline whose GLP1R designs have activated the receptor in cAMP assays (a dual GCGR/GLP1R cyclic agonist at EC50 32 nM). Four runs against the 207-residue fragment, 300 iterations each: run 1 (15 aa linear, best iteration 206), run 2 (15 aa cyclic, converged to the ALAWCVNFIEDRAPS family), run 3 (20 aa cyclic, stopped at 245 of 300 but converged by iteration ~229) and run 4 (12 aa cyclic, 298 iterations, converged to IVGETCPVKCFC). The length sweep is the result: 15 aa is the sweet spot. 15 aa gave three hits at ipSAE 0.83–0.88; 20 aa gave none (best 0.780, groove-only, binder pLDDT 33–55); 12 aa gave none (best 0.802 with zero groove contacts, pLDDT 23–55). One honest method note: runs 1 and 2 were launched without --receptor_if_residues, so EvoBind picked its own site on the whole fragment — and picked the orthosteric region anyway. The campaign's peptide c2-run1-b206 (MLIRYFVNQQRNYNP) went on to carry the full 6/6 geometry at 20.6 Å and is the only non-RFD4 peptide in the final twenty.

C3 — BoltzGen cyclic peptides, including the c4 scale batch (2026-10-20; promising). Tools: BoltzGen 0.3.2, Boltz-2, IPSAE, reactifpTM. A second, independent peptide generator at the same site. Four batches: batch 1 on the groove+junction constraint (7 single-design runs, all weak), batch 2 on the junction alone (the c1 lesson, and the better batch), batch 3 twelve more junction designs, batch 4 — logged as campaign 4 — thirty more. 55 designs screened; 7 two-domain HITs. Two findings of lasting value. First, the junction-only constraint transferred from a different generator: deeper reach (tm 1–4, ecl3 4–7) and better sample consistency. Second, BoltzGen's own metrics ranked its best designs wrongly (its ipTM 0.21–0.41 against our 0.77–0.86) — the measurement behind doctrine 2 of chapter 4. Operationally: the pipeline fits a 12 GB card only at one design per run with a fresh output directory, because retries into the same directory accumulate state (a failed 10-design run made the next "1-design" retry regenerate all 11 and die at 13.9 GiB). Four of the first six perfect activation geometries came from this campaign's junction batches.

C5 — BindCraft2 peptides (2026-10-20; promising). Tools: BindCraft2, Boltz-2, IPSAE. A third generator at the junction, 50 trajectories, 15–18 aa, with BindCraft2's gates deliberately relaxed so that raw output would reach our independent screen. BindCraft2 accepted 0 of 50 by its own gate. 18 designs screened on our pipeline, 4 two-domain HITs — and one of them, c5-bc2-l18_bfe509d11b1b8f27 (ipSAE 0.861), was the best design in the challenge at that date. The lineage still records this campaign's verdict detail as "Pending full screening", which is stale: the campaign tables and notes/best-per-campaign.md carry the finished numbers.

C6 — SolubleMPNN re-sequencing of the c1 champions (2026-10-20; record). Tools: SolubleMPNN (run from the LigandMPNN checkout with --model_type soluble_mpnn), Boltz-2, IPSAE. This campaign exists because of c1's poly-alanine failure and one tool measurement: SolubleMPNN produces 28 % mean alanine where ProteinMPNN produced 47 % on the same backbone. Five champion backbones (e1b2-r0036, e1-r0014, e1b-r0059, e1-r0025, e1b-r0037), binder residues within 4.5 Å of the receptor pinned, only the periphery redesigned at temperature 0.1, 8 sequences per backbone, 40 designs folded. 20 samples cleared the two-domain bar — the challenge's running total went from 49 to 80 in one campaign. c6-e1-r0025-s2 reads ipSAE 0.934 with the full groove (6 of 6 groove residues), the highest ipSAE of the whole challenge; c6-e1b-r0059-s5 took the composite lead at 19.42 with the deepest reach recorded at the time (groove 5/6, tm 4/4, ecl3 8/8). The finding: one backbone produced a whole family better than the original on affinity, groove coverage and reach — the measured repeat of a challenge-2 precedent.

C7 — extended-length peptides, 20–24 aa (2026-10-20; partial). Tools: BoltzGen, Boltz-2, IPSAE. The one untried length class, everything else held at c3's best configuration. 30 designs sampled, 5 two-domain HITs. Verdict: viable, not superior. Longer peptides cover more of the groove — two of them touch all six groove residues, which no 15 aa peptide did — but they do not beat the 15–18 aa band on affinity (best 0.834 against 0.934). No design from this campaign carries the 6/6 geometry, and none entered the submission. An honest negative with a clear cause.

C8 — the junction recipe at scale (2026-10-21; promising). Tools: BoltzGen, Boltz-2, IPSAE, the activation-geometry gate. This campaign exists because of one measurement: the gate's first full rescore said the c3 junction-only configuration had produced 4 of the 6 perfect geometries in the whole pool. So the identical spec was run 60 more times. The yield held: 3 more 6/6 designs — c8-run41 (6/6 at 21.0 Å, 5/5 agreement), c8-run13 (6/6 at 17.6 Å, 4/5, and also a two-domain HIT — the strongest both-lens design of the time) and c8-run20 (6/6 at 18.1 Å but only 1/5 agreement, flagged). 105 of 300 samples landed in the deep tier. The activation pool went from six designs to nine. c8-run13, a 13-residue peptide, is in the final twenty.

C9 — re-sequencing the 6/6 miniprotein (2026-10-21; record). Tools: SolubleMPNN, Boltz-2, IPSAE, the activation-geometry gate. The c6 recipe applied to the one c1 design that carried the full activation geometry: e1b2-r0065, the 84-residue miniprotein, 47 interface positions pinned. 33 variants folded. 5 carry the full 6/6 pattern, several deeper than the parent, and 13 are two-domain HITs. c9-e1b2-r0065-s4 (ipSAE 0.911, 5/6 at 21.2 Å) led the campaign and entered the 2026-10-21 twenty. (Record conflict: the README, notes/campaign-tables-2026-10-23.md and notes/best-per-campaign.md all describe this campaign as "SolubleMPNN on c3 champions", while lineage.json, every design id in it and the viewer page viewers/multiview/c9-solublemnn-resequenced.html say the parent is e1b2-r0065, a campaign-1 design. The primary record wins: the parent is the c1 miniprotein. The selector's family label for these designs is solublemnn-c3, which is where the confusion comes from.)

C12 — RFD4-Proteina on NVIDIA's hosted GPU pool (2026-10-22; record). Tools: RFD4-Proteina (hosted), Boltz-2, IPSAE, the activation-geometry gate. The strongest open generator the project had not used, available free on NVIDIA's Hugging Face Spaces until 2026-11-04, conditioned on the deep message region (TM pocket and ECL3) — the half of the activation span no earlier generator had reached. 256 designs across a medium-thinking and a high-thinking round, 8 designs per request, design segment 60–100 residues, receptor 1–409 fixed in the annotated CIF (inputs/rfd4-c12.yaml). The spec's hotspot atom selections name the message region explicitly — T298, R299, N300, W306, R380 and L384, written in fold numbering (fold n = UniProt n − 23) as residues 275, 276, 277, 283, 357, 361. Every design re-folded against the full construct by the same pipeline as everything else. 27 carry the full 6/6 geometry, 68 are two-domain HITs, and 769 of 1,280 samples are deep — the best rate the target had seen on both axes. c12-b3-d01 reads 6/6 at 22.0 Å with 5/5 agreement, ipSAE 0.899, pDockQ2 0.450 and pLDDT 83.3. Two operational notes: only the dedicated GPU pool works (the free ZeroGPU tier refused an 8-design medium request at 462 s), and the Space requires a signed-in browser session — an API token does not pass its gate, which was verified in the Space's own source (campaigns/c12-rfd4-proteina/README.md).

The re-sequencing loop in one picture. Left: c12-b21-d08, the 81-residue RFD4-Proteina champion (6/6 at 20.1 Å, 5/5, ipSAE 0.869). Right: c12-mpnn-b21-d08-v1, the interface-pinned SolubleMPNN variant of the same backbone — the interface residues within 4 Å are held fixed and only the periphery is redesigned, so the pose is preserved by construction (6/6 at 20.3 Å, 5/5, ipSAE 0.869, pLDDT 79.8 against the parent's 79.1). Both are in the submitted twenty; this pass produced the best full-geometry yield of the challenge, 25 of 81. Each panel comes from its own campaign's viewer page, so the receptors were superposed onto the left panel's frame (CA RMSD 5-7 A, the folds' own conformational spread) and all panels share one camera; the binder is magenta, the receptor blue.

C12 re-sequencing — SolubleMPNN on every full-geometry backbone (2026-10-22; record). Tools: SolubleMPNN, Boltz-2, IPSAE, the gate. The c6/c9 recipe applied to all 27 of c12's 6/6 champions: interface residues within 4 Å pinned, the top three deduped variants per backbone (confidence-ranked and pin-verified), 81 variants folded. 25 carry the full 6/6 pattern — 31 %, the best full-geometry rate of any single pass in the challenge, generator rounds included. 26 are two-domain HITs; 328 of 405 samples deep. Four of these variants are in the final twenty.

C13 — RFD4 conditioned on the ECD–TMD junction (2026-10-22; record). Tools: RFD4-Proteina (hosted), Boltz-2, IPSAE, the gate. The test of the split rule on the new generator: condition on the junction block alone — K197, Q210, Q221, Q234 — instead of the deep region, same length band, same everything else (inputs/rfd4-c13-junction.yaml, notes/c13-junction-2026-10-22.md). 73 designs; 15 carry the full 6/6 geometry — 21 %, the best full-geometry rate of any generator configuration in the challenge — 27 two-domain HITs, and 285 of 365 samples (78 %) in the deep tier. It produced the overall best design, c13-junction-b43-d02: 6/6 at 19.2 Å with 5/5 agreement, ipSAE 0.918, pDockQ2 0.471, pLDDT 86.2 (the highest in the submitted set), and a two-domain HIT. Seven of the twenty submitted designs come from this round. The split rule now had three independent confirmations: RFdiffusion3 (c1), BoltzGen (c3/c8) and RFD4-Proteina (c13).

C14 — RFD4 at the short length band, 40–70 aa (2026-10-23; record). Tools: RFD4-Proteina (hosted), Boltz-2, IPSAE, the gate. The deep conditioning at the size class campaign 1 had proven, generated against a trimmed target (inputs/target-trimmed-150-432.cif, contig 40-70, /0, B150-409) and folded against the full construct as always (inputs/rfd4-c14-short-deep.yaml). 72 designs; 6 full 6/6 geometries, 13 two-domain HITs — 18 %, the best two-domain rate of any round — and 162 of 360 samples deep. Two designs entered the twenty: c14-short-b46-d02 and c14-short-b47-d08, both 42 residues, tied at 92.2. The finding: the short band is a genuinely different and useful design class — fewer perfect geometries, more real binders.

8. How the designs were evaluated, and how "better" was decided

The evaluation moved three times, and each move is on the record with its reason. This matters more than the final formula: the ranking changed when a measurement said it should.

Composite v1 — reach-weighted (2026-10-18, campaign 1): tm*3 + ecl3*1.5 + ipSAE. Reach dominates because reach is the agonism proxy; affinity is a term, not the key. Used to pick c1's twenty.

Composite v2 — the meta-analysis update (2026-10-19): ipSAE*3 + pDockQ2*2 + LIS + tm*2 + ecl3. Driven by two things: the corrected pDockQ2 column, and the 3,766-binder finding that ipSAE-family metrics are the best predictors of real binding (campaigns/c2-peptide-agonists/README.md). Re-ranking the pool on v2 put three peptides into the twenty.

The rubric composite — activation first (2026-10-21 onward). The organizers published the prompt their own selector uses, and notes/submission-selection-2026-10-21.md records what it changes: the row order of the design file is the ranking; evidence for the hardest goal beats a strong score on an easier one; at least three screens must be recorded per design (pLDDT, ipSAE, mean Kyte-Doolittle hydropathy); method novelty counts. For GLP1R the hardest goal is activation, so the composite was rebuilt around it:

total = 2·A + 1.5·B + 1·E + 0.5·R, each term capped at 5.0, maximum 25.0; the reported score is that total rescaled to 0–100 (campaigns/c8-deep-junction/scripts/select-top20.py).

term weight bands
A — activation evidence 2.0 6/6 with ≥ 80 % of samples deep = 5.0; 6/6 at ≥ 60 % = 4.5; 6/6 below that = 4.0; 5/6 = 3.5 (+0.5 at ≥ 80 % agreement); 4/6 = 2.0; shelf tier = 1.5; groove tier = 1.0; wrong face = 0. A depth above 30 Å costs 1.0
B — binding 1.5 ipSAE ≥ 0.90 = 5; ≥ 0.85 = 4; ≥ 0.80 = 3; ≥ 0.75 = 2; else 1. +0.5 if pDockQ2 ≥ 0.30, capped at 5
E — expression risk 1.0 the mean of a pLDDT band (≥ 70 = 5, ≥ 60 = 4, ≥ 50 = 3, else 2) and a hydropathy band (−0.5…0.5 = 5, −1…1 = 4, else 3)
R — reach 0.5 (groove/6 + tm/4 + ecl3/8) / 3 × 5 — the fraction of the activation path recovered

Ties break on insertion agreement, then depth.

The hard quality gate, applied before ranking — because the composite under-weights the things that make a design untestable: pLDDT ≥ 63, pDockQ2 ≥ 0.18, and no low-complexity sequence (entropy ≥ 2.5 bits, no residue above 45 % of the chain, no homopolymer run of 6 or more). It removes 486 of the 800 scored designs and leaves 314 eligible. The script's own comment records why the floors exist: they used to be applied by hand to the chosen twenty, and the selector "could and did return designs below them — including a 24-residue poly-alanine tract that scored 88.4".

Diversity is a preference, not a gate. The note's reading of the organizers' "25 % per track" was later corrected — the 25 % allocates screening capacity between tracks, it is not a per-family cap, and the selection prompt itself is not public ("will be published after the competition"), so its treatment of within-submission similarity is unknown. The selector therefore fills by score and uses the family count only to order designs that tie on total, so diversity never costs a better-scoring design its slot. Near-duplicates are rejected outright: a sequence ≥ 90 % identical to one already kept, at equal length, is skipped. That rule lives in one place now, because an earlier version had the selector and the submission builder filtering differently and producing two different sets of twenty.

One bug worth naming. The family function used to prefix-match with startswith("c1-"), which matched no campaign numbered 10 or above — so every c12/c13/c14 design fell into one shared "other" bucket and the per-family cap discarded most of them. The fix anchors the match on the text before the first dash. The three best campaigns of the challenge were being penalised by a string comparison.

What the final sort actually did. Ranking the 314 eligible designs by total and admitting down the list produced the twenty in submission/competition-submission-rubric-2026-10-23.csv. Four designs in the top 24 by score are not in the file: c12-mpnn-b32-d03-v2 (rank 14 by score, pLDDT 48.2), c12-b22-d02 (rank 16, pLDDT 52.2) and c12-mpnn-b22-d02-v3 (rank 17, pLDDT 58.9) all sit below the 63 pLDDT floor; c12-mpnn-b3-d01-v2 (rank 20) is also absent, and the records do not say whether the floor or the 90 %-identity check against its parent c12-b3-d01 removed it. The cut is tight: the twentieth entry scores 87.8 on a total of 21.96, and the first design below the line is c9-e1b2-r0065-s4 at 21.94 — campaign 9's champion missed the final file by 0.02 composite points, having been in the 2026-10-21 twenty.

9. How the designs aim at activation, not just at binding

This is objective 2, the one with no public predictor, and it runs through every stage of the project:

  1. The epitope choice is the whole bet. The organizers recommended the groove. The published record says groove occupancy produces antagonists. So every campaign after the first batch conditioned on the junction or deeper — and the measurement justified it three times on three different generators (c1 25 % vs 14 %, c3/c8 on BoltzGen, c13's 21 % full-geometry rate on RFD4).
  2. The screen tests the footprint, not only the score. A design needs a groove contact and a TM-pocket contact and zero clashes to be called a hit. A high ipSAE on the groove alone is labelled groove-only and ranks accordingly.
  3. The full receptor is always the fold target. Never the extracellular domain alone, because the public attempts show that a binder designed against a cut-down target clashes into the bundle that was removed — and the clash column is what makes that visible.
  4. The activation evidence is weighted twice as heavily as binding (2.0 against 1.5) and four times as heavily as reach, because the organizers' own prompt says evidence for the hardest goal wins.
  5. The gate means what the lab means. Its cutoffs were declared before any design existed and calibrated on four experimental structures whose pharmacology is known — a full agonist, a biased full agonist, another full agonist, a weak partial agonist — plus a groove-only negative control that reads 0/6. A design scored 6/6 at 20 Å is being compared with GLP-1's own 6/6 at 20.59 Å.
  6. Reach that comes from wrapping is not reach. The second lens and the 30 Å threshold exist to catch exactly that, and they disqualified three of the four designs that reached the pool's likeness ceiling.
  7. The honest limit. Every statement above is a structural prediction. The cAMP reporter assay decides. What can be said is that the selection loop was built, from the gate's calibration onward, to prefer designs that reproduce the hormone's own activating geometry at the hormone's own depth, and that the submitted set carries the strongest such geometries the project produced.

What the set looks like. Seventeen of the twenty carry the full 6/6 activation pattern and three carry 5/6 — and the three 5/6 designs are there because the composite weights binding and expression alongside activation: e1-r0025 and c12-b27-d08 and c13-junction-b40-d01 all read ipSAE ≥ 0.90. All seventeen 6/6 entries score the maximum 5.0 on the activation term, meaning at least four of their five samples land in the deep tier. Insertion depths span 17.6 to 29.3 Å around the hormone's own 20.6 Å. ipSAE runs 0.840 to 0.933, pDockQ2 0.186 to 0.471, pLDDT 63.4 to 86.2, and the normalized score 87.8 to 95.4 (submission/methodology.md). Lengths run 13 to 96 residues: two peptides (13 and 15) and eighteen miniproteins (42–96).

By origin. Seventeen of the twenty come from the three RFD4-Proteina rounds — eight from the deep message-region round (four of them re-sequenced variants), seven conditioned on the ECD–TMD junction, two from the 40–70 aa band. The other three are one RFdiffusion3 miniprotein (e1-r0025), one EvoBind peptide (c2-run1-b206) and one BoltzGen junction peptide (c8-run13) — six method families in all. The campaigns that contributed nothing to the file are c3, c5, c6, c7 and c9, and their campaign-level findings are what the later rounds were built on.

The prescreen on the shipped file (records/prescreen-report-rubric-2026-10-23.csv): 18 pass, 2 no_reference_signal (the two peptides, under the tool's 25-residue floor). Target similarity 0.00 on nineteen entries and 0.095 on c14-short-b47-d08; every cluster size is 1; no entry is a known binder or a near-match to one.

11. What is honest, and what the records do not agree on

The limits.

  • Nothing here is wet-lab validated. No assay result, no upload receipt, and no wet-lab number of our own appears anywhere in the tree. The affinity and EC50 values quoted in chapters 2 and 6 are literature values from the research brief, not measurements of ours.
  • Agonism has no validated in-silico predictor, and ours is a geometry proxy. The gate measures whether a design reproduces one reference agonist's pharmacophore at depth. It is calibrated, declared in advance and reproduced on four experimental structures — and it is still a structural proxy against a single reference pose. A different agonist pose would shift every number.
  • The gate scores the pose it is given. Five-sample pose agreement is the mitigation the scorer's own documentation recommends; it is not a solution.
  • No design is agonist-like in absolute terms. The pool ceiling on the harsh 19-contact lens is 6 of 19, and the submitted leaders sit at 3–5. The full hormone touches all 19.
  • The one method that would have aimed generation at the pattern was never run. The reward-guided RFD4 route was coded and shelved on memory; the upside it represented is unmeasured.
  • The receptor is folded, not embedded. No membrane is modelled; the depth axis is derived from the receptor's own rim and floor residues precisely because of that.
  • Five of twelve campaigns contributed no submitted design. They are reported above with their numbers, not quietly dropped.

Where the records disagree with each other. In each case the primary record (lineage.json, records/, submission/) is preferred and the conflict is named:

  1. Campaign 9's parent backbone. The README, notes/campaign-tables-2026-10-23.md and notes/best-per-campaign.md call it "SolubleMPNN on c3 champions"; lineage.json, every design id (c9-e1b2-r0065-*) and the viewer page say the parent is e1b2-r0065, a campaign-1 design. The primary record is right; the prose notes inherited the selector's family label solublemnn-c3.
  2. Campaign 1's design count. notes/strategies.md says 77 designs folded from 183 backbones; notes/campaign-tables-2026-10-20.md and lineage.json's protein list say 57; the final rescore table and records/selection-scores-2026-10-23.csv say 67. The 67 is the count the shipped selection actually scored and is used here; the records do not reconcile the three figures.
  3. Campaign 7's design count. The campaign README and notes/best-per-campaign.md say 30 designs sampled; the lineage summary, the campaign tables and the gate rescore say 18. The selection record carries 30 boltzgen-long-peptide rows, which is exactly why the project total is 800 in records/ and 788 in the campaign table — the 12-design difference is entirely c7.
  4. What "deep" means. notes/campaign-tables-2026-10-23.md defines deep as "samples that insert (depth ≤ 30 Å)", and submission/methodology.md calls the agreement figure "the number of samples that insert at all, our declared 30 Å depth threshold". Neither is the scorer's definition: activation_geometry.py assigns the deep tier at depth ≥ 16.0 Å with ≥ 3 features satisfied, and the 30 Å number is the separate wrap-pose penalty. The distinction is checkable in the data — c6-e1b-r0037-s3 reads "5/6 d49.9 5/5", which would be impossible under a ≤ 30 Å rule.
  5. The deep-sample column of notes/campaign-tables-2026-10-23.md changes units mid-table. The c1–c7 rows count designs (53/67, 9/15, 34/55, 13/18, 30/40, 10/18) while the c8–c14 rows count samples (105/300, 95/165, 769/1280, 328/405, 285/365, 162/360). Its total row, 1,893/3,447, matches neither sum: the numerator adds the mixed column (149 + 1,744), and 3,447 corresponds to no denominator in the table (designs would give 213, samples 1,065 + 2,875 = 3,940). The per-campaign figures from c8 on are internally consistent and are the ones quoted above; the total is not used.
  6. The two-domain HIT counts do not agree between the records. For campaign 8 the lineage summary says 14 two-domain samples, its chapter outcome says 11 HITs, the campaign table says 12 and the commit message for the round says 11. For campaign 3 the lineage and notes/best-per-campaign.md both say 7 HIT designs while the campaign table says 9. For campaign 1 the campaign notes say 39 HIT samples across 21 designs while the table says 26. The likely cause is that the notes count HIT designs and the 2026-10-23 table counts something else per campaign, but no record states the column's definition. Campaign-level HIT numbers in this document follow the campaign's own note; the table's 222 total is quoted only as a total.
  7. Campaign 5's verdict is stale in the lineage. verdict_detail still reads "Pending full screening", though the campaign finished with 18 designs screened and 4 HITs.
  8. The 2026-10-21 selection note is superseded, and says so. Its "Final outcome" section describes a twenty that campaigns 12–14 later displaced, and it records two of its own misreadings (the 25 % rule and the availability of the selection prompt). The shipped file and the 2026-10-23 tables are authoritative.
  9. The likeness-driven swap did not survive. c12-mpnn-b13-d01-v3 was swapped into the twenty on 2026-10-22 as the only design to pass both lenses; the 2026-10-23 pure-score rebuild dropped it (it scores 85.2, rank 56 of 800). The same rebuild dropped campaign 9's c9-e1b2-r0065-s4, which notes/best-per-campaign.md still describes as having "entered the submission twenty".
  10. c2-run1-b206's pDockQ2 reads 0.217 in the campaign-2 decision table and 0.358 in every later table and in the shipped record. The later value is from the corrected column (the screen's "pDockQ2" had been reading pDockQ until 2026-10-19); the early number should be read as pDockQ.
  11. "c8-deep-junction" is a misleading name. The campaign ran the c3 junction-only cyclic-peptide spec unchanged; "deep" refers to the gate's depth tier, not to a different hotspot set. The campaign tables call it "deep conditioning", which invites the wrong reading.

Folder structure

challenges/03-glp1r/
├── README.md        this document
├── lineage.json     the campaign record the local web app renders
├── docs/figures/    the figures embedded above, plus a self-contained HTML build
├── campaigns/       one directory per campaign: its scripts, specs and results
├── notes/           the dated working log, the strategy notes and the campaign tables
├── records/         the selection scores and the final ranking
├── submission/      the uploaded CSV, the methodology and the design-method text
├── inputs/          committed target files and reference structures
├── viewers/         Mol* multiview pages, one per campaign
├── videos/          rendered clips
└── submission-package-2026-10-2{2,3}.zip   the packages as uploaded

The fold outputs themselves live outside the repo under ~/c3-work/.
